deep_reading.title: Is 2:4 Sparsity Still Worth It? Semi-Structured Sparsity versus Quantization in LLM Inference
deep_reading.content:
Since Ampere, NVIDIA GPUs have supported 2:4 sparsity: in a matrix multiplication, one operand keeps only two non-zeros in every four elements along the reduction axis, and the tensor cores nominally run twice as fast. It can be stacked with quantization, so the real deployment question is: from the current precision, should the next step be adding 2:4 or dropping to the next lower precision? This paper by an independent researcher compares the two on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B, at "equal storage bits (with the sparsity position index counted)" and at "equal nominal compute tier", across all six GEMM operand families of a transformer layer, and times them on three GPU generations (L40S, H100, RTX PRO 6000), over 220,000 configurations in all. The conclusion is blunt: ==as long as a lower precision is available, adding 2:4 is both less accurate and slower==. Only at the lowest precision the hardware supports (FP8 on Ada and Hopper) does 2:4 earn its place: on an H100, a 2:4 plus FP8 model served by vLLM gets 27% higher prefill throughput than dense FP8 with GSM8K accuracy on par. But that model was retrained on 13 billion tokens; one-shot pruned models are unusable.

## 1. The problem: hardware still supports it, software has given up

On one side, NVIDIA has kept sparse tensor cores in every GPU generation, and Blackwell added sparse FP4; on the other, in 2026 vLLM and LLM Compressor removed 2:4 support because too few people used it. A split this wide shows that a direct comparison on real hardware is missing.

Existing pruning-versus-quantization comparisons mostly compare at "nominal compression", mostly for weights, and do not time "add 2:4" against "drop one precision" on the same GPU. The author points out four things that are easy to miss. First, 2:4 stores a position index next to every kept value, so it costs more than half the bits of its dense counterpart. Second, both approaches promise twice the throughput, but the datasheet does not say how much each actually delivers. Third, most operands at inference time (activations, Q, K, V, attention probabilities) are computed on the fly and must be pruned and compressed before every GEMM, a cost invisible if you time only the GEMM. Fourth, the hardware fixes which operand can be sparse and along which axis, so whole-tensor statistics (such as kurtosis) miss what 2:4 actually removes.

## 2. How to compare fairly

The first yardstick is equal bits, for comparing memory savings. Each format is charged for every bit it stores per original element: values, indices and scales. 2:4 keeps half of the elements but adds a 1-bit index per original element, so it saves less than half of the bits. The result is that "2:4 on 2m-bit values" costs exactly as much as "dense (m+1)-bit": 2:4 with INT8 costs the same as dense INT5, 2:4 with INT4 the same as INT3, and 2:4 with FP16 costs more than FP8.

![Equal-bit pairings (paper Figure 1). Each line joins two formats of equal cost, e.g. 2:4 with INT8 and INT5 both cost 5.125 bits per element; 2:4 with FP16 costs more than FP8.](figs/2610.28947/fig1_equal_bits.png)

So at equal storage, the real choice is "drop half the elements and store the rest at twice the precision" versus "keep all elements with one more bit each".

The second yardstick is equal compute tier, for comparing speedups: pair formats by datasheet nominal throughput. The 2x tier is 2:4 with FP16 against dense FP8 or INT8; the 4x tier is 2:4 with FP8 against dense 4-bit floating point, which only Blackwell has.

Under both yardsticks, accuracy is operator-level relative error against an FP32 reference output. The author defines R as "error of the best 2:4 configuration" divided by "error of the best quantized configuration"; R below 1 means 2:4 is better. To favour neither side, each picks the best from an equal-effort menu: the 2:4 side tries magnitude pruning, Wanda and SparseGPT, the quantized side tries round-to-nearest, GPTQ and AWQ, all calibrated on the same C4 data. Speed uses cuSPARSELt sparse GEMMs, and for operands computed on the fly both sides pay for online pruning or online quantization.

## 3. While a lower precision exists: dropping one step always wins

On accuracy, at equal bits 2:4 loses at every storage budget on both models. At 8 bits the error gap is over an order of magnitude; it shrinks as bits fall but never flips, and the closest case still has R just above 1. At equal tiers it is clearer: in the 2x tier, 2:4 with FP16 has five to sixteen times the error of dense FP8, for all six operand families. Across all compute comparisons, the few cases 2:4 wins are against weak formats (MXFP4 with power-of-two scales, and row-wise INT8); against FP8 and NVFP4 it never wins.

Operator error is not model quality, so the author also ran whole-model tests on the 15 configurations closest to parity, the most favourable cases for 2:4. On GSM8K, 2:4 is never significantly better than quantization and is significantly worse 7 times. Where 2:4 does better on perplexity or RULER, it is mostly on attention probabilities: keeping the top two of every four scores sharpens attention, which helps long-context retrieval and perplexity but never helps reasoning.

Measured speed is just as unfavourable to 2:4. The table gives "rival time divided by 2:4 time"; above 1 means 2:4 is faster (Llama-3.1-8B projections, median over 2K to 16K tokens):

| GPU | 2x tier W | 2x tier X | 4x tier W | 4x tier X | 2:4 added on FP8 | 2:4 added on NVFP4 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| L40S | 0.89 | 0.89 | – | – | 1.65 | – |
| H100 | 0.74 | 0.80 | – | – | 1.42 | – |
| RTX PRO 6000 | 0.84 | 0.85 | 0.66 | 0.70 | 1.33 | 1.40 |

W means the weights are sparse; X means the activations are sparse (online preprocessing counted on both sides). The first four columns are all below 1, which means that of two approaches promising the same nominal speed, dense lower precision delivers more in practice. On H100, 2:4 with FP16 runs at only 74% of dense FP8's speed.

![Error vs. throughput (paper Figure 5, Qwen3-8B). The x-axis is throughput relative to dense BF16, the y-axis operator error; lower right is better. The grey region means some other format is both faster and more accurate. Top row: sparse weights; bottom row: sparse activations.](figs/2610.28947/fig5_pareto.png)

Putting accuracy and speed together, as long as a lower dense precision is available, every 2:4 configuration falls in the grey region: some dense format is faster and several times more accurate. 2:4 reaches the frontier only at the far right, once stacked on top of the lowest precision.

How online pruning is implemented also matters. The author wrote a fused kernel that reads the input once and writes kept values and indices once, running near memory-copy bandwidth; cuSPARSELt's own prune-and-compress path and PyTorch's semi-structured conversion are several times slower and eat most of what the sparse GEMM saves. Attention probabilities P are even worse: after online pruning and compression, 2:4 runs at about half the dense speed, so P cannot be used as a standalone sparse operand.

## 4. Why it loses: the deleted energy cannot be won back

The reason is a simple asymmetry. Quantization keeps every value and only rounds it; each added bit halves the error. 2:4 deletes half the values outright; what is deleted is gone, and no number of bits on the remaining values brings it back. The author calls the sum of squares of the two dropped values in each group of four, as a share of the tensor's total sum of squares, the "2:4 energy loss". For i.i.d. Gaussian data it is 13.2%, independent of bits. On Gaussian data the 2:4 side's error stays at 36% to 37% across budgets, while the dense format of equal bits goes from 0.6% at INT8 to 27.4% at INT3. The two would cross only below 3 bits, a precision no dense tensor core supports.

Combining this energy loss with the quantization error gives a predicted R computed straight from the tensor with no fitted parameters. Its rank correlation with measured R is 0.93, and it separates 2:4 wins from losses with an AUC of 0.95. But 2:4 wins at only 3% of points, so the criterion explains how big the gap is and why, not who wins a close call. For contrast, the whole-tensor kurtosis proposed in earlier work barely correlates with the outcome. ==What decides the contest is the local structure of the tensor along the hardware's grouping axis, not its overall distribution==.

The analysis also predicts the effect of Hadamard rotation (a common outlier-removal step before low-bit quantization). Rotation makes the four elements in each group more alike, raising the energy loss, while narrowing the quantization range. In measurements, rotation roughly doubles R for Q, K and linear-layer inputs, and the criterion predicts the direction of change at 87% of points. Most real deployments rotate, so the paper's unrotated results are actually optimistic for 2:4.

## 5. At the lowest precision: a real speedup, but only with retraining

At the FP8 or NVFP4 floor there is no lower dense format to switch to, so 2:4 can only be stacked on top, and at this point it has no rival. The author makes the linear-layer weights 2:4, keeps attention in BF16, and uses the base Llama-3.1-8B. Linear-layer GEMMs with 2:4 on FP8 run 1.3x to 1.7x faster, the first time in the paper that 2:4 really wins.

End-to-end vLLM results on one H100; the 2:4 model is Sparse-Llama (a 2:4 Llama retrained on 13 billion tokens):

| Configuration | Weight memory (GiB) | Prefill (k tok/s) | Decode b=1 (tok/s) | Decode b=64 (tok/s) | GSM8K |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Dense BF16 | 15.0 | 41.4 | 136 | 6,424 | 0.596 |
| 2:4 BF16 | 9.3 | 40.7 | 115 | 6,477 | 0.624 |
| Dense FP8 | 8.5 | 58.9 | 198 | 8,556 | 0.568 |
| 2:4 FP8 | 6.1 | 74.6 | 234 | 9,914 | 0.612 |

2:4 plus FP8 has 27% faster prefill than dense FP8, 18% and 16% faster decode at batch 1 and 64, and 28% less weight memory. The end-to-end gain is smaller than the GEMM-level 1.42x because attention and the other layers do not shrink. Serving the same weights with dense kernels removes the speedup, so the gain comes entirely from the sparse kernels. In BF16, vLLM's 2:4 path is no faster than dense, and slower at batch 1.

The GSM8K column needs care. With only 250 problems, at around 0.6 accuracy the standard error is about 3 points, so the gap between 0.568 and 0.612 is within noise, and the author also reports no significant difference. And the 2:4 model and the dense model have different training histories, so all one can say is "no worse", not "2:4 is more accurate".

The real cost is retraining. The table gives WikiText-2 perplexity and GSM8K accuracy (250 problems):

| Floor | Dense | One-shot 2:4 | Retrained 2:4 (13B tokens) | Author's retraining (1B tokens) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| BF16 | 6.31 / 0.600 | – | 8.13 / 0.612 | 8.19 / 0.300 |
| INT4 weights | 6.90 / 0.540 | 18.61 / 0.032 | 8.45 / 0.580 | 8.53 / 0.292 |
| FP8 | 6.36 / 0.552 | 17.82 / 0.028 | 8.19 / 0.632 | 8.25 / 0.308 |

One-shot pruning is unusable on every floor: perplexity more than doubles and GSM8K drops to about 3%, which means the model has essentially lost its reasoning. The author's own distillation retraining from the dense model on 1 billion FineWeb-Edu tokens catches up with Sparse-Llama on perplexity (8.25 vs. 8.19) but gets only half its GSM8K (0.308 vs. 0.632).

![Retraining (paper Figure 7). (a) Which elements element-wise 2:4 and Blackwell FP4's pairwise 4:8 keep; (b) perplexity keeps falling with retraining tokens; (c) GSM8K largely stalls after the first 0.25 billion tokens; the star is Sparse-Llama, retrained on 13 billion tokens.](figs/2610.28947/fig7_retrain.png)

==Perplexity overstates how much retraining has recovered==: perplexity is mostly back within the first 0.25 billion tokens while reasoning is far from back, and the perplexity curve gives no hint of how far there is to go. Judging whether a sparse model's retraining is done requires a reasoning task. Sparsifying only some layers does not avoid retraining either: applying 2:4 to half the linear-layer compute, chosen from lowest predicted cost upward, buys only 1.14x to 1.25x.

## 6. Blackwell's sparse FP4 is harder to use

Blackwell's sparse FP4 is not element-wise 2:4 but "pairwise 4:8": each group of eight elements is split into four adjacent pairs, and two of the pairs are kept. The author verified on an RTX PRO 6000 that element-wise masks give wrong results in this format. Its kernels run 1.4x faster than dense NVFP4, but keeping pairs discards more than keeping elements, because both elements of a pair must stay or go together and cannot each be chosen by size. On Gaussian data its energy loss is 20.8%, and after one-shot pruning perplexity reaches 108.83, five times that of element-wise 2:4.

Existing models do not help either. Sparse-Llama, trained for element-wise 2:4, cannot be converted directly; conversion discards a third of its trained weights and breaks the model. With the author's 1-billion-token retraining budget, GSM8K recovers only to 0.132, against 0.460 for dense NVFP4, so at this budget it is not usable.

## 7. Limits and practical takeaways

- Only two 8B models. The Blackwell conclusion is limited by 1 billion tokens and one untuned retraining recipe; whether longer retraining recovers it is not tested.
- The 4-bit integer weight floor (mainly for decode) is not timed, because vLLM removed the matching sparse kernels. Decode is bound by memory bandwidth, where 2:4 saves only bytes, which helps on some GPUs and hurts on others.
- In the speed comparisons, sparse GEMMs get an exhaustive tuning search while the dense side uses the library's default heuristics, which favours 2:4, and 2:4 still loses.

If the hardware still offers a lower precision (e.g. BF16 to FP8 on H100), drop the precision first; do not add 2:4. If you already deploy in FP8, prefill throughput is the bottleneck, and a well-retrained 2:4 model is available, 2:4 can give a real 20–30% speedup, but vLLM mainline has removed support, so you will be maintaining your own branch. On Blackwell, there is no ready pairwise 4:8 model yet, and the cost and outcome of retraining your own are not assured. When evaluating any retrained sparse model, do not rely on perplexity alone.

BF166.31 / 0.600–8.13 / 0.6128.19 / 0.300

6. Blackwell's sparse FP4 is harder to use

Blackwell's sparse FP4 is not element-wise 2:4 but "pairwise 4:8": each group of eight elements is split into four adjacent pairs, and two of the pairs are kept. The author verified on an RTX PRO 6000 that element-wise masks give wrong results in this format. Its kernels run 1.4x faster than dense NVFP4, but keeping pairs discards more than keeping elements, because both elements of a pair must stay or go together and cannot each be chosen by size. On Gaussian data its energy loss is 20.8%, and after one-shot pruning perplexity reaches 108.83, five times that of element-wise 2:4.

Existing models do not help either. Sparse-Llama, trained for element-wise 2:4, cannot be converted directly; conversion discards a third of its trained weights and breaks the model. With the author's 1-billion-token retraining budget, GSM8K recovers only to 0.132, against 0.460 for dense NVFP4, so at this budget it is not usable.

7. Limits and practical takeaways

  • Only two 8B models. The Blackwell conclusion is limited by 1 billion tokens and one untuned retraining recipe; whether longer retraining recovers it is not tested.
  • The 4-bit integer weight floor (mainly for decode) is not timed, because vLLM removed the matching sparse kernels. Decode is bound by memory bandwidth, where 2:4 saves only bytes, which helps on some GPUs and hurts on others.
  • In the speed comparisons, sparse GEMMs get an exhaustive tuning search while the dense side uses the library's default heuristics, which favours 2:4, and 2:4 still loses.

If the hardware still offers a lower precision (e.g. BF16 to FP8 on H100), drop the precision first; do not add 2:4. If you already deploy in FP8, prefill throughput is the bottleneck, and a well-retrained 2:4 model is available, 2:4 can give a real 20–30% speedup, but vLLM mainline has removed support, so you will be maintaining your own branch. On Blackwell, there is no ready pairwise 4:8 model yet, and the cost and outcome of retraining your own are not assured. When evaluating any retrained sparse model, do not rely on perplexity alone.

deep_reading.title: SGLang Low-Latency Mode: Kernels and Runtime
deep_reading.content:
At low concurrency, such as a coding or agent app where one user has only one or two sessions open, each request has very little to compute per step, and latency goes mostly to kernel launches, idle gaps between kernels and multi-GPU communication. In this LMSYS blog post, the SGLang, NVIDIA and AMD teams introduce SGLang Low-Latency Mode: a plugin framework that ==brings vendor kernels, heavily fused for specific models and hardware, into SGLang without merging that code into the SGLang main repository==. The test model is DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with DSpark speculative decoding. In AgentX agent-trace replay, on four NVIDIA GB300 GPUs with one concurrent session, P90 per-user generation speed rises from 671.2 to 928.4 tokens/s (1.38x); on four AMD MI355X GPUs with four sessions, from 331.6 to 516.0 tokens/s (1.56x). Both baselines are standard SGLang on the same hardware. This is an engineering blog, not a paper; the numbers are measured by the authors' own teams with no third-party reproduction.

## 1. The problem: at small batch sizes, time is not spent computing

With one request, DSpark verifies only six token rows per step. The matrix multiplications themselves are fast; what takes time is a chain of small kernels queuing one after another, the gap as each kernel starts and drains, and the waits during tensor parallelism's two cross-GPU reductions (adding up each GPU's partial results) per layer, when the GPU computes nothing. At large batch sizes these costs are spread over lots of computation; at small ones they dominate.

Deep fusion tuned to a specific model, hardware and concurrency can remove these gaps, but each combination needs its own implementation. There are several generations of NVIDIA and AMD hardware, model architectures differ, and so do parallel layouts; putting all of it in the SGLang main repository would keep growing the code and review burden. So the post really covers two things: how each vendor built low-latency kernels, and how SGLang plugs them in without taking on the maintenance load.

## 2. NVIDIA: almost the same number of kernels, much less waiting

NVIDIA's implementation is called sgl-nvidia-mega. The authors first profiled one decoder layer under a warmed CUDA graph, one request, taking medians over about 800 measurements per arm:

| Region of one decoder layer | SGLang | With plugin | Saved |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Attention (from previous MoE output to output projection) | 33.4 µs | 18.3 µs | 15.1 µs |
| Attention output projection and tensor-parallel reduction | 10.9 µs | 9.4 µs | 1.5 µs |
| MoE (from routing to reduced output) | 44.4 µs | 36.5 µs | 7.9 µs |
| Whole layer | 96.8 µs | 68.4 µs | 28.4 µs |

The whole layer is 29% faster, and more than half of that comes from the attention region. Most notably, the kernel count for one verify step only drops from 1,205 to 1,189. So ==the speedup does not come from merging kernels into fewer ones, but from overlapping consecutive kernels and waiting less==. The post also warns that profiling affects timings and region medians do not add up to the whole layer; the table explains the mechanisms and does not represent serving performance.

Four specific changes:

1. **Start the next kernel early.** CUDA's PDL (programmatic dependent launch) lets a kernel start while its predecessor is still running, preparing barriers and loading weights before waiting for input. SGLang already used PDL; the plugin moves the "you may start" signal earlier. Attention begins gathering KV before waiting for the query, and RoPE is applied while loading the query, removing a separate kernel.
2. **Send results out at the end of the matrix multiply.** After the attention output projection, each GPU has only a partial sum that must be reduced across GPUs. Previously the matrix multiply wrote its result to memory, and the next kernel read it back and sent it to the other GPUs. The plugin lets each thread block, as soon as its tile is done, write it straight from registers to the other GPUs via NVLink multicast, without waiting for the whole multiply to finish and without the extra read-back.
3. **Start expert computation before routing finishes.** With at most eight rows, each expert's selected tokens fit in one eight-row tile; the plugin places them with a bitmap and counts, no scanning or sorting, and launches the first expert matrix multiply early. This is where the MoE region's 7.9 µs saving comes from.
4. **Put draft sampling in one kernel.** DSpark's draft head proposes five tokens in sequence, previously one launch each. The plugin does all five in one launch per GPU, cutting the draft stage from 85.1 µs to 34.2 µs with acceptance logic unchanged.

![Where the cross-GPU send happens after the attention output projection (blog figure). Top: standard SGLang writes the partial sum to memory, and the next kernel reads it back and sends it to four GPUs; bottom: the plugin multicasts to four GPUs directly from the end of the matrix multiply. Both use two kernels; box sizes do not represent time.](figs/sglang-low-latency/nvidia-output-handoff.png)

On a fixed workload of 8K input and 1K output, with simulated mean acceptance length 3.51 and one to eight concurrent requests, per-user decode speed rises 12% to 38%. The lower the concurrency, the bigger the gain, which matches the analysis above: what is saved is a fixed waiting cost, and the fewer the requests, the larger its share.

![Per-user decode speed vs. total throughput per GPU (blog figure, 4×GB300, 8K in / 1K out). Grey is plugin off, blue is plugin on; points on the two lines correspond from one to eight requests.](figs/sglang-low-latency/nvidia-low-concurrency.png)

This figure carries one more conclusion the post does not state. With the plugin on and two requests, per-user speed is about 840 tokens/s, faster than the roughly 745 tokens/s with the plugin off and one request, while total throughput per GPU rises from about 165 to about 325 tokens/s. In other words, a service with a hard latency target can double its concurrency with the plugin and still be no slower per user than before.

## 3. AMD: only two persistent kernels per layer

AMD's implementation, sgl-amd-mono, supports MI355X and MI350X and takes a different route. The authors see three main costs at low concurrency on AMD. First, even with HIP graphs removing CPU-side launch work, each small kernel still costs 2 to 4 µs on the GPU. Second, in the gap while one kernel drains and the next ramps up, compute units sit idle and weight loading pauses. Third, during the two cross-GPU all-reduces per layer no computation runs.

![Schematic timeline of one DeepSeek-V4.1 layer at batch size 1 (blog figure). Top: the standard path runs dozens of small kernels with a gap at every boundary and stops computing during two all-reduces; bottom: the plugin merges the layer into two launches, K1 and K2, loads routing-independent weights early, and sends partial sums to other GPUs while computing.](figs/sglang-low-latency/amd-mono-layer.png)

The plugin uses FlyDSL (a tool for writing GPU kernels on the AMD side) to merge most of a layer into two persistent kernels. K1 does the mHC update, Q/KV projections and KV cache writes; K2 does attention, output projection, MoE and both all-reduces. One launch boundary is kept between them so that K1's KV writes are visible across the GPU before K2 reads them.

Inside a kernel, stages hand off through "values tagged with the decode step": each value a stage produces carries the current step number, and the next stage, on the same GPU or another, starts as soon as the tag matches, with no separate flag and no per-step reset. Weights that do not depend on routing load early; expert weights load once the router has picked the experts. The all-reduce is also brought into the kernel: each finished output tile is pushed to every GPU, each GPU sums in a fixed order, and other workgroups keep computing meanwhile.

This carries a risk: if one GPU stalls, all GPUs wait inside the kernel. So every cross-GPU wait has a deadline shorter than SGLang's watchdog; on timeout all GPUs abort that launch together instead of hanging the whole server.

## 4. The plugin framework: specialized kernels live outside the main repository

External kernel libraries connect in four steps. First, registration: for each supported model architecture, the library declares its requirements and build entry point. Second, checks: before loading weights, SGLang verifies that hardware, precision, parallelism and so on are compatible, failing early rather than mid-run. Third, build: weights and resources are prepared at initialization, finished before the KV cache is sized, so the plugin's memory is accounted for and does not compete with the KV cache. Fourth, runtime dispatch: a plugin may cover only some step types and token counts, and uncovered steps fall back to SGLang's original forward. All GPUs must agree on whether a step uses the plugin, or they will enter mismatched collective communication. The path chosen during CUDA graph capture is recorded, so replay needs no Python-side decision.

The benefit is that vendor teams can iterate independently while SGLang maintains only the interface. The cost is that external kernels bypass SGLang's normal code review, so correctness must be backstopped by tests at the interface, and the post says those tests are still planned.

## 5. Results on an agent workload

AgentX trace replay simulates real agent sessions; the metric is P90 per-user generation speed, both sides using 4-GPU tensor parallelism with DSpark, toggling only the plugin.

![AgentX replay results (blog figure). Grey is standard SGLang, blue is low-latency mode.](figs/sglang-low-latency/figure-1.png)

| Hardware | 1 session | 4 sessions | 8 sessions |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 4 × GB300 | 1.38x | 1.28x | 1.20x |
| 4 × MI355X | 1.50x | 1.56x | 1.45x |

On NVIDIA the gain shrinks as concurrency rises, consistent with the fixed-workload results. On AMD all three levels are above 1.45x, highest at four sessions. One possible reason is that AMD's standard path starts lower: at one session its baseline is about 405 tokens/s, only about 60% of the GB300 baseline, so there are more gaps to squeeze. The two vendors differ in both hardware and kernel approach, so these numbers are not suited to comparing which hardware is faster.

## 6. Limits and practical takeaways

- Only the DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash plus DSpark combination is supported for now; GLM-5.3, K3, MiniMax M3 and others are in development.
- No accuracy comparison is given, only that speculative decoding's acceptance logic is unchanged. Fused kernels may change the order of floating-point operations (for example, the order of cross-GPU sums), and the post does not say whether results match the standard path exactly.
- CI and performance regression tests for the plugin interface are still planned, and the interface itself is early and will change.
- The gains are concentrated at one to eight concurrent requests. At large batch sizes these costs are already spread thin, and the post gives no data there.

If your service is low-concurrency and sensitive to per-user latency, and you happen to deploy DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on GB300 or MI355X, you can try this mode directly. For other models, the method is the more useful part: at small batch sizes, profile each layer's timeline first to see whether time goes to computing or waiting; if it is waiting, prioritize kernel overlap and earlier communication rather than simply cutting the kernel count. Isolating specialized kernels outside the main framework via plugins is also a maintenance approach worth borrowing.

papers.title: RCSD: Reinforcement and Continual Learning for Domain-Specific Speculative Decoding
papers.authors: Mingkang Liu, Weiming Meng, Peipei Jiao, Jiawei Zhang, Tianyuan Liu, Junyan Li, Lichen Pang
papers.summary: Hisense's RCSD continues training a speculative-decoding draft model that was distilled with HASS, using DPO or GRPO: sequences from the target alone are "good," sequences alternating target and draft are "bad," and the GRPO variant scores by acceptance rate. On Qwen3-1.7B and Llama-3.1-8B, acceptance length exceeds HASS on four datasets and draft steps 3–6—for example Qwen3-1.7B on GSM8K at step 6 rises from 2.176 to 3.246, and Llama-3.1-8B ShareGPT throughput from 142.3 to 176.6 token/s. ==The paper reports no generation-quality evaluation==.

deep_reading.title: RCSD: Reinforcement and Continual Learning for Domain-Specific Speculative Decoding
deep_reading.content:
Speculative decoding works like this: a small draft model guesses several tokens ahead, and the large model checks them all in one parallel pass, keeping every guess it agrees with. The average number of tokens kept per round is the "acceptance length". The longer it is, the fewer rounds the large model has to run, and the faster generation becomes. Draft models are usually trained by distillation, i.e. pushed to match the large model's whole output distribution. This paper from Hisense argues that this is the wrong target: ==verification only asks whether the draft's token is the one the large model would also pick, so the draft only needs to get the top few candidates in the right order, not reproduce the whole distribution==. The proposed RCSD (a framework that keeps training the draft model with reinforcement learning) starts from a conventionally trained draft model and continues training it with DPO or GRPO. All training data is generated by the large model itself, with no human labels and no extra reward model. On Qwen3-1.7B and Llama-3.1-8B, acceptance length beats the baseline in every test setting. However, the abstract's "35% average improvement" and "1.35x end-to-end speedup" do not match the paper's own tables, as shown below.

## 1. The problem: what the draft model learns is not what it is used for

The paper has a single baseline, so it is worth being clear about it. In EAGLE, the draft model is tiny, and besides the tokens generated so far it reads the large model's hidden states directly to guess the next word. HASS (a distillation method for training EAGLE draft models) is the baseline, and RCSD also continues from a trained HASS draft model.

The distillation loss is forward KL divergence. Its character is "cover everything": any token the large model gives even a little probability to must also get some probability from the draft, or the draft is penalised. The trouble is that the draft is orders of magnitude smaller than the large model and lacks the capacity to learn the whole distribution. So its capacity gets spread over many low-probability tokens that will never be chosen.

The authors illustrate the mismatch in the figure below. Acceptance depends only on whether the draft's favourite token matches the large model's favourite. Bottom left is the ideal case: the distributions are close and the peaks line up. Bottom right, the draft's distribution is far from the large model's and the KL loss is high, but the peaks still line up, so the token is accepted anyway. The top two panels are the opposite: the peaks are misaligned, so the token is rejected whether KL is high or low. In other words, KL loss is only an indirect proxy for acceptance, and not a very accurate one.

![KL loss and acceptance length do not agree (paper Figure 1). The solid line is the large (base) model's distribution, the dashed line the draft model's. Top left: low KL but peaks misaligned, rejected; top right: high KL and peaks misaligned, rejected; bottom left: low KL and peaks aligned, accepted; bottom right: high KL but peaks aligned, still accepted.](figs/2610.29527/fig1_kl_vs_accept.png)

So the authors change the goal. Instead of asking the draft to "imitate the whole distribution", they push it to concentrate probability on the path the large model is most likely to take, giving up the tail if necessary. In the paper's words, the draft moves from covering every mode (mode-covering) to grabbing the main one (mode-seeking).

## 2. Method: use the large model's own output as the positive example

Both training variants start from a trained HASS draft model and keep a frozen copy of these initial weights as a reference, so the new model cannot drift too far.

The DPO variant needs pairs of "good" and "bad" sequences. The good one is generated entirely by the large model token by token, representing what the draft ideally should have guessed. The bad one is generated by alternation: the large model writes 1 token, then the draft writes k tokens in a row without checking, then the large model writes 1 again, and so on. The draft's own stretches tend to drift away from what the large model would write, so this sequence is a natural negative example. Training raises the draft's probability of the good sequence relative to the reference and lowers its probability of the bad one.

One detail matters a lot here: the tokens in the bad sequence that the large model wrote are masked out of the loss. Without the mask, training would also push down these tokens, which are correct by construction. In addition, DPO is sensitive to sequence length, so the same mask positions are applied to the good sequence too, keeping the number of compared tokens equal on both sides.

The GRPO variant compares a whole group instead of a single pair. For each prompt there is one sequence generated directly by the large model and several in which the draft writes 1, 2 or 3 tokens at a time. Each sequence's score is the sum of two parts, each first standardised within the group. One is how natural the large model finds the sequence, measured by its log-probability under the large model, i.e. the sum of the log of each token's probability. The other is how many of the draft's tokens in it the large model would accept. Sequences scoring above the group average are reinforced, those below are weakened.

![The RCSD framework (paper Figure 3). Left: during speculative decoding, verification splits the output into accepted and early-rejected parts; top right (A): DPO variant, sequences generated by the large model are positives, sequences alternating between large model and draft are negatives; bottom right (B): GRPO variant, a group of sequences scored by acceptance rate. Bottom: after training, the draft's distribution concentrates on the large model's high-probability tokens.](figs/2610.29527/fig3_overview.png)

What both variants share is that positives, negatives and scores are all produced automatically by the large model, so data can be built in bulk from live requests or any text prompts. ## 3. Result one: acceptance length grows in every setting

Testing uses HumanEval (code), MT-Bench (multi-turn dialogue), GSM8K (maths) and the remaining ShareGPT, so only the last one matches the training distribution, which matters later. | Model | Steps | HASS | HASS + DPO | HASS + GRPO | GRPO relative gain |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Qwen3-1.7B | 3 | 2.12 | 2.57 | 2.57 | +22% |
| Qwen3-1.7B | 6 | 2.26 | 2.97 | 3.00 | +33% |

| Llama-3.1-8B | 6 | 2.78 | 3.26 | 3.29 | +18% |

| MT-Bench | 90.6 | 134.2 | 141.9 | 143.1 | 1.07x |

An 11% longer acceptance length giving only 7% more speed is also expected. Each round includes not only drafting but also the large model's verification and scheduling overhead, which does not shrink when guesses get better. papers.summary: Scitix.AI's UlaCache maps every GPU KV pool and CPU memory into one logical address space so ==GPU and CPU each store different history==, and removes MLA's cross-GPU duplication under TP; the GPU pool is shared across requests with a bucketed parallel LRU for eviction. Under SGLang + GLM-5.3 with 64K–128K inputs, concurrent decodeable requests on 8×B300 TP rise from HiSparse's 37 to 452; with speculative decoding, peak throughput is 1.16–2.51× HiSparse. deep_reading.title: UlaCache: Unified Logical Addressing for Sparse LLM Serving
deep_reading.content:
Models such as DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and the GLM-5 family use index-based sparse attention: at each decoding step a scoring module picks a small subset of past positions, and attention reads only the KV cache at those positions. Each step reads less data, but storage does not shrink, because a position skipped at this step may be picked at the next one, so the whole history has to stay. With long contexts and many requests, how much history fits in memory decides how many requests can decode at once. Scitix.AI's UlaCache puts every GPU's KV pool and optional CPU memory into one "logical address space": the inference engine allocates and selects KV by logical address only, and UlaCache decides which GPU or CPU holds the data, moves it, and updates the mapping. ==The core idea is not "use more CPU" but "make every byte of memory hold different history, not copies"==. On SGLang with GLM-5.3 and 64K–128K-token long-document summarization requests, with speculative decoding on and equal memory budgets, peak throughput is 1.16x to 2.51x that of HiSparse. The paper's own curves show that almost all of this gain comes from fitting more requests at once; per-step speed at the same batch size does not improve.

## 1. The problem: most memory holds duplicate copies

The authors first measured how GLM-5.3 allocates KV on 8×B300 and found heavy duplication in both existing approaches, from two sources.

The first source is duplication across GPUs. GLM-5.3 uses MLA, which compresses the KV of all attention heads into one shared representation. Standard tensor parallelism (TP) splits computation across GPUs by attention head, but that shared representation cannot be split by head, so every GPU stores a full copy. Under 8-way TP only 12.5% of the space holds distinct history; the other 87.5% is copies. In other words, eight GPUs' worth of memory gives the storage capacity of one.

The second source is duplication between GPU and CPU. HiSparse is the current reference design for extending sparse-attention KV into CPU memory: it keeps full histories on the CPU and, at each step, moves the selected entries to the GPU and caches them. The catch is that every entry cached on the GPU is still on the CPU too. In the figure it uses 53.3 million physical slots but stores only 30.0 million distinct history positions. Its 23.3 million GPU slots make access faster without adding any history capacity.

![GLM-5.3 KV allocation on 8×B300 (paper Figure 2, speculative decoding off). (a) Under TP, only 12.5% of SGLang's and HiSparse's space holds distinct history; (b) SGLang stores 27.1 million positions on GPU only, while HiSparse stores 30.0 million full-history positions on CPU plus 23.3 million GPU slots holding copies of some of them.](figs/2610.29820/fig2_replicas.png)

HiSparse also has an allocation problem: it gives each request a fixed-size GPU cache. When there are few requests, the freed memory cannot be used by the others. The authors' example is 8×B300, DP mode, speculative decoding on, a single request: the GPU could hold the entire history, but one request's quota cannot, so it keeps fetching from the CPU. As a result its time per output token (TPOT) is 23.5% higher than GPU-only SGLang.

## 2. Unified logical addresses: the engine tracks "which number", not "where"

UlaCache gives each KV entry a fixed logical address and keeps a mapping table recording which GPU slot or CPU slot currently holds it. When data moves between GPU and CPU, only the mapping changes; the logical address stays the same, so the engine side never needs to know the data moved. This is the same idea as PagedAttention mapping logical blocks to physical GPU blocks, extended from one GPU to several GPUs plus CPU.

In DP mode each GPU serves its own requests and manages its own GPU pool and CPU pool; a request's capacity is the sum of the two. What this removes is GPU–CPU duplication: an entry lives either on the GPU or on the CPU, never both.

TP mode changes more. All GPUs' pools form one distributed address space, and each GPU stores only part of each request's history: logical address t goes to GPU t mod P, where P is the number of GPUs. Eight GPUs now hold eight different slices of history instead of eight identical copies. The cost is that computation must fetch data from other GPUs, so each computing GPU keeps a local buffer of recently selected KV. Sparse attention picks heavily overlapping positions across consecutive steps, so the buffer hit rate is high and most of the time only a few missing entries need fetching.

![Memory pooling and the local buffer in TP mode (paper Figure 4). Logical addresses alternate between GPU 0's and GPU 1's pools; this step GPU 0 selects positions 2, 4 and 5: 2 is already in the local buffer and reused, 4 comes from its own pool, and 5 comes from GPU 1's pool over CUDA IPC.](figs/2610.29820/fig4_tp_pooling.png)

Two more details are worth noting. Some layers in GLM-5.3 share one sparse selection result; UlaCache does the address lookup and deduplication once for such a group and, while the current layer computes, uses a separate CUDA stream to prefetch data for the later layers. The index keys used by the scoring module are also spread across GPUs by the same rule: each GPU scores only its local keys, and one all-gather combines the scores. This removes duplicate scoring but adds communication wait at low concurrency.

## 3. PB-LRU: what to evict from a shared GPU pool

With CPU storage enabled, the GPU pool is no longer carved up per request; all requests share it, recently used entries stay on the GPU and long-unused ones move to the CPU. That needs a replacement policy. Standard LRU keeps a timestamp per slot and scans the whole pool to choose victims. Doing that at every decoding step and every layer puts the cost on the critical path of decoding.

PB-LRU (the authors' Parallel Bucketed LRU) avoids the scan with an approximation. Instead of ordering slots exactly, it puts every slot accessed in the same scheduling round into the same "bucket". Each layer group keeps a ring of recent buckets plus one cold bucket. Each round the current bucket advances one position, and whatever remains in the old bucket about to be reused moves to the cold bucket; only the labels change, no data moves. When space is needed it uses free slots first, then the cold bucket, then recent buckets from oldest to newest. The current bucket is never chosen, because its data is about to be used by this step's attention.

Each bucket is a bitmap with one bit per GPU slot. On top sit several layers of summary bitmaps, where each bit says whether the segment below has any occupied slots, so selection can skip whole empty segments. Hit detection, recency updates and deduplication all run in parallel on GPU threads. Data movement also has an ordering rule: move the data first, then update the mapping and signal completion; attention waits for the signal before reading new locations, so it never reads half-moved data.

## 4. Experiments: capacity grows several-fold, throughput follows

Experiments use GLM-5.3 (FP8 weights and KV cache) on 8×H200 and 8×B300. Baselines are SGLang with all KV on GPU and HiSparse with history on CPU; speculative decoding uses MTP. For fairness, all three systems get the same GPU memory and the same CPU budget (128 GB per H200, 192 GB per B300). The workload is Multi-LexSum long-document summarization with 64K to 128K input tokens; contexts are long enough that KV storage is the main pressure.

First, how many requests fit at once. The table gives admitted requests from paper Figure 8 (speculative decoding on):

| Setup | SGLang | HiSparse | UlaCache | UlaCache vs HiSparse |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 8×H200 TP | 6 | 25 | 70 | 2.8x |
| 8×H200 DP | 29 | 197 | 213 | 1.1x |
| 8×B300 TP | 36 | 37 | 363 | 9.8x |
| 8×B300 DP | 260 | 295 | 566 | 1.9x |

The gap is largest in TP mode, because that is where the 87.5% of cross-GPU copies is removed. In DP mode HiSparse already keeps history on the CPU, so on H200 the gain is only about a tenth. B300 DP nearly doubles because B300 has large GPU memory, and once GPU and CPU stop duplicating each other the freed space is substantial.

![Effective KV capacity (top, millions of slots, solid = GPU, hatched = CPU) and admitted requests (bottom) (left half of paper Figure 8).](figs/2610.29820/fig8_capacity.png)

Once capacity grows, the question is whether it turns into throughput. With speculative decoding on, peak throughput over HiSparse is 1.16x on H200 DP, 1.70x on H200 TP, 1.73x on B300 DP and 2.51x on B300 TP. With it off, B300 TP peak is 3.51x SGLang's.

![Output throughput across batch sizes (paper Figure 7). Blue is UlaCache, orange HiSparse, purple SGLang; crosses mark batch sizes a system cannot fit.](figs/2610.29820/fig7_throughput.png)

This figure says more than the peak numbers. At batch sizes where both curves exist, UlaCache and HiSparse almost overlap, so per-step speed has not improved. The gap appears after HiSparse's curve ends: it cannot fit more requests, while UlaCache keeps climbing. On B300 TP, admitted requests rise almost 10x but throughput only 2.51x, because past a certain batch size the throughput curve flattens and more requests no longer buy proportional speed. The one exception is H200 DP with speculative decoding: only 8% more requests but 16% more throughput. The curve shows HiSparse dipping at large batches, which fits the explanation that its fixed quotas lower the hit rate.

At low concurrency, across eight configurations with batch sizes 1 to 8, UlaCache's TPOT is lower than HiSparse's but higher than GPU-only SGLang's. The reason is the extra address lookup, scheduling and, under TP, cross-GPU communication. A separate PB-LRU test replays the same access traces on 8×H200 DP: its GPU hit rate is within 0.1 percentage points of exact LRU, so the bucket approximation loses almost nothing in cache quality. At larger batches its scheduling is 1.5x to 2.3x faster. But when little replacement is needed, exact LRU is actually faster, because PB-LRU still maintains bucket labels.

## 5. Limits and where it applies

- One model and one workload: GLM-5.3 on long-document summarization. Different sparse selection patterns (tasks with less step-to-step overlap) would change buffer and GPU-pool hit rates, which the paper does not cover.
- Throughput comparisons take each system's best value over all batch sizes, and the best points fall at different batch sizes. So "2.51x" reflects how many requests fit, not being faster under the same load. If your production concurrency never reaches the baseline's capacity limit, you will get little of this gain.
- At low concurrency it is slower than GPU-only SGLang. For latency-sensitive, low-concurrency serving, the GPU-only setup is still the better fit.
- No accuracy test. UlaCache does not change which positions attention selects, so in principle the output is unchanged, but correctness of cross-GPU fetches and swaps rests on the implementation; no consistency check is reported.
- No report of CPU–GPU bandwidth use, and no comparison with other concurrent sparse-attention KV offloading systems.

## 6. Practical takeaways

If you serve MLA plus sparse attention models such as GLM-5 or DeepSeek-V4.1 on SGLang, with long contexts and the bottleneck being "memory cannot fit more concurrent requests", the most useful lesson here is to check for duplicate storage first. When deploying an MLA model with TP, work out how much KV on each GPU also exists on the others. By the paper's count it is 87.5% under 8-way TP, and removing it gains more capacity than adding CPU memory.

Second, when extending into CPU memory, make GPU and CPU hold different data and let all requests share the GPU pool instead of giving each a fixed quota. Finally, when evaluating such systems, look at the curves at equal batch sizes, not just peak multiples. The former tells you whether each step got slower; the latter only tells you how many more requests fit.

Under 8-way TP only 12.5% of the space holds distinct history; the other 87.5% is copies. In other words, eight GPUs' worth of memory gives the storage capacity of one.

The second source is duplication between GPU and CPU. HiSparse is the current reference design for extending sparse-attention KV into CPU memory: it keeps full histories on the CPU and, at each step, moves the selected entries to the GPU and caches them. The catch is that every entry cached on the GPU is still on the CPU too. In the figure it uses 53.3 million physical slots but stores only 30.0 million distinct history positions. Its 23.3 million GPU slots make access faster without adding any history capacity.

HiSparse also has an allocation problem: it gives each request a fixed-size GPU cache. When there are few requests, the freed memory cannot be used by the others. The authors' example is 8×B300, DP mode, speculative decoding on, a single request: the GPU could hold the entire history, but one request's quota cannot, so it keeps fetching from the CPU. As a result its time per output token (TPOT) is 23.5% higher than GPU-only SGLang.

2. Unified logical addresses: the engine tracks "which number", not "where"

UlaCache gives each KV entry a fixed logical address and keeps a mapping table recording which GPU slot or CPU slot currently holds it. When data moves between GPU and CPU, only the mapping changes; the logical address stays the same, so the engine side never needs to know the data moved. This is the same idea as PagedAttention mapping logical blocks to physical GPU blocks, extended from one GPU to several GPUs plus CPU.

In DP mode each GPU serves its own requests and manages its own GPU pool and CPU pool; a request's capacity is the sum of the two. What this removes is GPU–CPU duplication: an entry lives either on the GPU or on the CPU, never both.

TP mode changes more. All GPUs' pools form one distributed address space, and each GPU stores only part of each request's history: logical address t goes to GPU t mod P, where P is the number of GPUs. Eight GPUs now hold eight different slices of history instead of eight identical copies. The cost is that computation must fetch data from other GPUs, so each computing GPU keeps a local buffer of recently selected KV. Sparse attention picks heavily overlapping positions across consecutive steps, so the buffer hit rate is high and most of the time only a few missing entries need fetching.

Two more details are worth noting. Some layers in GLM-5.3 share one sparse selection result; UlaCache does the address lookup and deduplication once for such a group and, while the current layer computes, uses a separate CUDA stream to prefetch data for the later layers. The index keys used by the scoring module are also spread across GPUs by the same rule: each GPU scores only its local keys, and one all-gather combines the scores. This removes duplicate scoring but adds communication wait at low concurrency.

3. PB-LRU: what to evict from a shared GPU pool

With CPU storage enabled, the GPU pool is no longer carved up per request; all requests share it, recently used entries stay on the GPU and long-unused ones move to the CPU. That needs a replacement policy. Standard LRU keeps a timestamp per slot and scans the whole pool to choose victims. Doing that at every decoding step and every layer puts the cost on the critical path of decoding.

PB-LRU (the authors' Parallel Bucketed LRU) avoids the scan with an approximation. Instead of ordering slots exactly, it puts every slot accessed in the same scheduling round into the same "bucket". Each layer group keeps a ring of recent buckets plus one cold bucket. Each round the current bucket advances one position, and whatever remains in the old bucket about to be reused moves to the cold bucket; only the labels change, no data moves. When space is needed it uses free slots first, then the cold bucket, then recent buckets from oldest to newest. The current bucket is never chosen, because its data is about to be used by this step's attention.

Each bucket is a bitmap with one bit per GPU slot. On top sit several layers of summary bitmaps, where each bit says whether the segment below has any occupied slots, so selection can skip whole empty segments. Hit detection, recency updates and deduplication all run in parallel on GPU threads. Data movement also has an ordering rule: move the data first, then update the mapping and signal completion; attention waits for the signal before reading new locations, so it never reads half-moved data.

4. Experiments: capacity grows several-fold, throughput follows

Experiments use GLM-5.3 (FP8 weights and KV cache) on 8×H200 and 8×B300. Baselines are SGLang with all KV on GPU and HiSparse with history on CPU; speculative decoding uses MTP. For fairness, all three systems get the same GPU memory and the same CPU budget (128 GB per H200, 192 GB per B300). The workload is Multi-LexSum long-document summarization with 64K to 128K input tokens; contexts are long enough that KV storage is the main pressure.

First, how many requests fit at once. The table gives admitted requests from paper Figure 8 (speculative decoding on):

The gap is largest in TP mode, because that is where the 87.5% of cross-GPU copies is removed. In DP mode HiSparse already keeps history on the CPU, so on H200 the gain is only about a tenth. B300 DP nearly doubles because B300 has large GPU memory, and once GPU and CPU stop duplicating each other the freed space is substantial.

Once capacity grows, the question is whether it turns into throughput. With speculative decoding on, peak throughput over HiSparse is 1.16x on H200 DP, 1.70x on H200 TP, 1.73x on B300 DP and 2.51x on B300 TP. With it off, B300 TP peak is 3.51x SGLang's.

This figure says more than the peak numbers. At batch sizes where both curves exist, UlaCache and HiSparse almost overlap, so per-step speed has not improved. The gap appears after HiSparse's curve ends: it cannot fit more requests, while UlaCache keeps climbing. On B300 TP, admitted requests rise almost 10x but throughput only 2.51x, because past a certain batch size the throughput curve flattens and more requests no longer buy proportional speed. The one exception is H200 DP with speculative decoding: only 8% more requests but 16% more throughput. The curve shows HiSparse dipping at large batches, which fits the explanation that its fixed quotas lower the hit rate.

At low concurrency, across eight configurations with batch sizes 1 to 8, UlaCache's TPOT is lower than HiSparse's but higher than GPU-only SGLang's. The reason is the extra address lookup, scheduling and, under TP, cross-GPU communication. A separate PB-LRU test replays the same access traces on 8×H200 DP: its GPU hit rate is within 0.1 percentage points of exact LRU, so the bucket approximation loses almost nothing in cache quality. At larger batches its scheduling is 1.5x to 2.3x faster. But when little replacement is needed, exact LRU is actually faster, because PB-LRU still maintains bucket labels.

5. Limits and where it applies

  • One model and one workload: GLM-5.3 on long-document summarization. Different sparse selection patterns (tasks with less step-to-step overlap) would change buffer and GPU-pool hit rates, which the paper does not cover.
  • Throughput comparisons take each system's best value over all batch sizes, and the best points fall at different batch sizes. So "2.51x" reflects how many requests fit, not being faster under the same load. If your production concurrency never reaches the baseline's capacity limit, you will get little of this gain.
  • At low concurrency it is slower than GPU-only SGLang. For latency-sensitive, low-concurrency serving, the GPU-only setup is still the better fit.
  • No accuracy test. UlaCache does not change which positions attention selects, so in principle the output is unchanged, but correctness of cross-GPU fetches and swaps rests on the implementation; no consistency check is reported.
  • No report of CPU–GPU bandwidth use, and no comparison with other concurrent sparse-attention KV offloading systems.

6. Practical takeaways

If you serve MLA plus sparse attention models such as GLM-5 or DeepSeek-V4.1 on SGLang, with long contexts and the bottleneck being "memory cannot fit more concurrent requests", the most useful lesson here is to check for duplicate storage first. When deploying an MLA model with TP, work out how much KV on each GPU also exists on the others. By the paper's count it is 87.5% under 8-way TP, and removing it gains more capacity than adding CPU memory.

Second, when extending into CPU memory, make GPU and CPU hold different data and let all requests share the GPU pool instead of giving each a fixed quota. Finally, when evaluating such systems, look at the curves at equal batch sizes, not just peak multiples. The former tells you whether each step got slower; the latter only tells you how many more requests fit.

papers.title: SPARE: Sparsity Allocation via Routing Entropy for Efficient MoEs
papers.authors: Yifan Yang, Hanling Yi, Dongquan Yang, Feng Lin, Rong Xiao, Aijun Li, Xiaotian Yu
papers.summary: Intellifusion's SPARE decides how many MoE experts to prune per layer: on calibration data it computes Top-K gate-weight entropy per token per layer, and ==layers whose weights are diffuse lose little when one expert is dropped, so they are pruned more==. It needs no training and composes with methods such as REAP that choose which experts to drop. Under the same selection method and budget, at 50% expert pruning Qwen3-30B-A3B's eight-task average rises from 57.2% to 63.8%, and DeepSeek-R1's math/code/science average from 80.1 to 82.8; on Mixtral it also beats uniform allocation.

papers.title: NormTune: Norm-Guided Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Reasoning-Intensive Tasks
papers.authors: Zhangming Li, Qinghao Hu, Weifan Guan, Yifan Zhang, Peisong Wang, Jian Cheng
papers.summary: CASIA finds that on reasoning tasks the ==weight-update norm of LoRA-style PEFT is far smaller than full fine-tuning==, and treats that as the main cause of the gap. NormTune adaptively amplifies under-updated layers by per-layer update norm. Training on S1K-1.1, rank-8 LoRA, Bone, and MoRA raise the average of AIME 2024, MATH 500, GPQA, and AIME 2025 by 24.24%, 11.33%, and 16.21%; at rank-256 all three match or slightly beat S1 full fine-tuning.

papers.title: FlashNext-RL: A System Optimization Study for Long-Horizon Agentic RL of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next
papers.summary: Snowflake specializes a training system for long-horizon software-engineering agent RL on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, based on prime-rl, generating trajectories with vLLM and training the full 48-layer model in BF16 on one 8×B200 node (==freezing the first two layers and other parts==). After host offload, gradient accumulation, and MoE/sparse-attention kernel work, per-GPU training throughput rises from about 395 to 4,438 token/s and context from 32K to 131K. papers.summary: CUHK-Shenzhen and collaborators propose TrainBridge to optimize training programs on Ascend NPUs: ==it first extracts optimization intent from execution produced by a GPU compiler stack (operator fusion, etc.)==, lets an agent rewrite the NPU program, then iterates from NPU profiles. papers.title: Looped Uniform Diffusion Language Models
papers.authors: Saiteja Utpala, Chieh-Hsin Lai, Yuki Mitsufuji, Praneeth Vepakomma
papers.summary: MBZUAI and Sony study "looping" in uniform diffusion LMs (any position may be replaced by any token and can be revised during generation): reuse the first few Transformer layers inside each denoising step with the training objective and sampler unchanged. On OpenWebText and FineWeb-Edu, matching the validation NLL of a non-looped model trained on ~0.5T tokens takes up to 2.8× and 3.3× less training compute; at equal function-call counts generation perplexity is up to 9.8% lower. ==Sampling smaller loop counts more often during training== lets downstream tasks use 12% fewer loops without accuracy loss.

papers.title: Sparsity Should Be ALLOTted by Output: Training-Free Allocation of Block-Sparse Attention for Video Diffusion Transformers
papers.authors: Tianze Xia, Xiaoling Zhou, Ruya Lan, Yiqiao Liao, Chengru Song
papers.summary: CASIA and Keling propose ALLOT to decide how many blocks a video diffusion Transformer's block-sparse attention keeps for each layer × denoising step: measure each cell's effect on final video error, then jointly solve densities under a measured latency budget without changing the existing block-selection policy or kernels. The authors observe that ==the most sensitive layer–step pairs are nearly unchanged across inputs==. At equal or lower latency with XAttention it beats every compared allocation; on HunyuanVideo PSNR rises 11.8 dB; on four published Wan2.1, Wan2.2, and HunyuanVideo pipelines, all nine settings meet or beat the default allocation.
